title: Coldline Lockdown
one_liner: Audits and locks down internet-reachable refrigeration controllers for independent grocers and food businesses.
speaker: Peter Diamandis
context: Hackers took over remotely managed supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe, switched them into defrost mode and spoiled the food. Authorities told operators to take the controllers off the open internet. Alex says legacy industrial control systems are being neglected.
customer: Independent grocers, small supermarket chains, convenience-store groups and restaurant groups in Europe and the US whose refrigeration is run by remote-access controllers
problem: Their fridge and freezer controllers were installed by a refrigeration contractor and are often reachable from the internet with default logins. One overnight attack can destroy stock, and nobody on staff knows the setup.
revenue_model: Per-site hardening visit or remote audit, about $600–$1,500 per store, then about $40 a month per store for alert monitoring and quarterly re-checks (estimate)
why_now: The episode describes a second wave of attacks across eight countries after hundreds of French stores were hit. Authorities have now told operators to act, and the hosts say AI makes attacks cheaper while defence still needs humans.
first_steps: Write a one-page 'is your freezer controller on the internet?' checklist and send it to 20 local grocers
Partner with one refrigeration contractor who can take on remote-access changes on site
Run two free audits in exchange for a written case study
cost_to_start: About 2 weeks and under $1,000 (checklist, insurance check, contractor partnership)
competition: OT/ICS security firms serve large utilities and manufacturers; refrigeration contractors offer remote monitoring but rarely security hardening for small shops
risks: Touching controllers without the installer's involvement could void warranties or spoil stock. It needs proper written authorization from each owner. Large chains will buy from established security firms.

tool.title: Freezer Door Check
tool.one_liner: A questionnaire that scores how exposed a store's refrigeration controls are and prints a fix list.
tool.demo: The store owner answers about 15 questions (who installed the controllers, is there a cloud or remote app, default password changed, VPN, alarms on high temperature, who gets the alarm at 3am). The page outputs an exposure score, a ranked fix list with plain-language steps, and a printable sheet to hand to their refrigeration contractor. They can also paste a CSV temperature log and see flagged sudden rises that look like a forced defrost.
tool.data_plan: Customer's own answers and their own temperature-log CSV. Incident figures from the episode are shown as context only.
acceptance: Answering 'default password unchanged' and 'no high-temp alarm' raises the exposure score and puts those two fixes at the top of the list
Pasting a sample CSV with a jump from -18°C to 10°C within an hour highlights that row as a suspected forced defrost
A 'Print for contractor' button produces a clean one-page checklist view
The episode incident figures appear in a sourced 'What happened' box labelled as reported on the podcast
The questionnaire is usable on a 390px-wide phone screen
